series.title: 启动路径修复后，继续扩大分块
series.note: 先降低固定调用成本，再处理大输入的设备耗时。

plan.strategy: Replace the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper (rejected by candidate admission because it hides the launch) with a self-contained contiguous Triton kernel plus a generic strided-view kernel, all in-place on the input buffer
plan.code_changes: New tmp/main.py: masked 1-D contiguous kernel (_rad2deg_contig_kernel, BLOCK=8192), unrolled rank<=8 strided kernel (_rad2deg_strided_kernel) with dimension collapsing for non-contiguous in-place writes, empty-tensor early return, run(A) returns A
plan.hypothesis: A direct kernel[grid] launch removes the ~150us/call host overhead visible in the parent result (0.17ms/call vs 0.018ms reference) and fixes the transposed/strided in-place semantics that failed 3/18 independent cases

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round in this workspace: establishes the per-workload latency of the lean direct-launch architecture versus the PyTorch reference

conclusion.root_cause: The candidate admission gate rejects the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic seed (no visible kernel[grid] launch), so the measured baseline is the simplest self-contained architecture: direct masked contiguous kernel plus a generic rank<=8 strided-view kernel. All 36 workloads pass, including the four strided correctness cases (7/15/23 and the odd-strided ones) that the parent failed. Latency is host-bound, not device-bound: 65us/call at n=1024 and 77us/call at n=16.7M, while the parent's OpProf device event is ~3.2us, so the remaining cost is Triton per-launch host work (~65us) versus the PyTorch reference at ~20us.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: First measured round in this workspace: no previous measurement to compare against. Against the harness reference the candidate is 0.313x geo-mean, and the per-workload latencies are nearly size-independent (65.4us at 1024 elements, 76.8us at 4096x4096), which localizes the gap to fixed per-call host overhead rather than device throughput.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Measure the launch path on the target: introspect the installed Triton 3.5.1/FlagTree JIT dispatch and microbenchmark alternative launch forms (full JIT dispatch vs cached CompiledKernel runner vs pre-resolved stream) plus a BLOCK sweep, to decide how much of the ~45us gap versus the reference is removable.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The seed's own device kernel is only ~3.2us; its 0.10x score came from ~150us of host wrapper cost per call, so on this stack host dispatch, not arithmetic, is the optimization target.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Replaced the FlagGems pointwise_dynamic wrapper with a self-contained kernel[grid] implementation and added an explicit strided in-place path, which is also what makes the strided correctness cases pass.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-call Triton JIT dispatch with a pre-bound launcher for the same compiled kernel, re-reading pointer, numel and current stream on every call
plan.code_changes: Dense path: first call per (dtype, data_ptr&15) does a normal kernel[grid] launch and warmup; later calls invoke the already-compiled kernel's generated NPU launcher directly with the per-call data_ptr, numel and current stream (bound via torch_npu._C._npu_getCurrentRawStreamNoWait, same value as the Triton driver wrapper). Kernel body, BLOCK=8192, strided path and empty/semantic handling unchanged. Added do_not_specialize on n_elements so the reused artifact is valid for any numel.
plan.hypothesis: Nearly all of the remaining per-call latency is Triton JIT dispatch, not device work: the device event is ~3.2us while every workload measured 65-77us, and a tight-loop probe of the pre-bound launcher plus raw-stream read measured 10.0us end to end versus 11.4us for torch.rad2deg_

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing per-call JIT argument binding, specialization, cache-key and global-version bookkeeping (measured ~53us/call versus ~8us for the pre-bound launcher plus ~0.4us for the raw current-stream read) should collapse the fixed per-call cost that made latency nearly size-independent at 65-77us

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed by measurement that the per-call cost was Triton JIT dispatch rather than device work: the pre-bound launcher plus raw current-stream read reproduces the reference's tight-loop cost (10.0us versus 11.4us) and the harness now reports 14.3-14.8us for the nine launch-bound workloads. The three 4096x4096 workloads stay at 76.7-77.1us because BLOCK=8192 leaves them device-bound (measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements at that tile, 0.85TB/s, versus an 18.9us reference at 3.5TB/s).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: removing per-call JIT dispatch collapses the fixed cost that made latency size-independent. Observed: the nine workloads of 1024/65536/1048576 elements dropped from 65.4-65.9us to 14.26-14.78us (speedup 1.21-1.30x against a 17.6-18.7us reference), matching the ~10us tight-loop floor of the pre-bound launcher plus harness measurement overhead. The three 4096x4096 workloads were predicted to be unchanged and were: 76.7/76.8/77.1us (speedup 0.239/0.256/0.374) because there the device, not the launch path, dominates. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.3126 -> 0.8607 (2.75x) and all 36 workloads still pass, so the expectation was met and the residual gap is fully localized to the large-tile device path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Right-size the tile per size class, since the remaining gap is entirely the three 4096x4096 workloads: they are device-bound at 76.7-77.1us with BLOCK=8192 (0.85TB/s measured on target), while the same kernel at BLOCK=32768 measured 29.0us for fp16 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32. Use BLOCK=32768 for the large class, keep 8192 for the mid class and a small tile for the <=2048 class.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this stack the Triton JIT dispatch (binder + specialization + cache key + global-version check, ~53us) is an order of magnitude larger than the kernel (3.2us), so a pre-bound launcher is the primary lever, not the arithmetic. The pre-bound C launcher with an integer pointer costs 7.7us versus 12.9us with a tensor argument, and the raw current-stream read costs 0.44us versus 4.6us through the Triton driver wrapper.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 removed the framework wrapper and fixed strided in-place semantics (0.31x). Round 2 kept the same kernel and tile and only changed how it is launched, which raised the geo_mean to 0.861 and left tile sizing as the single remaining device-side lever.

plan.strategy: Right-size the elementwise tile per size class while keeping the same kernel and pre-bound launch path
plan.code_changes: Added a tile-size ladder selected from numel inside run(): BLOCK=2048 for n<=2048, BLOCK=8192 for n<=131072 (unchanged for the mid class), BLOCK=32768 above that. The block is part of the launch-cache key and is passed to _bind so each class binds its own compiled kernel; kernel body, launch path, strided path and semantics unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound by an undersized tile, not by the launch path: with BLOCK=8192 the on-target probe measured 78.9us for 16.7M fp16 elements (0.85TB/s) versus 29.0us at BLOCK=32768 (2.3TB/s) and 32.8us for fp32 versus a 30.6us reference, while every workload at or below 1048576 elements is launch-bound and unchanged by tile size

expected_effect.mechanism: Amortising each program's prologue/epilogue over a 64KB tile instead of 16KB raises the large-class MTE throughput from the measured 0.85TB/s to 2.3TB/s, cutting the device-bound 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us; the smaller tile for tiny inputs removes wasted masked lanes

conclusion.root_cause: With the launch path fixed, the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by the kernel's per-element vector work at BLOCK=8192. Raising the tile to 32768 lifted the effective throughput from 0.85TB/s to ~2.4TB/s, which is why those workloads dropped to 27.9-31.0us.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: the large class was device-bound by an undersized tile and should drop from 76.7-77.1us to roughly 31-35us, with the launch-bound workloads unchanged. Observed: the three 4096x4096 workloads fell to 27.85us (fp16), 29.91us (bf16) and 31.00us (fp32), i.e. speedups 0.650/0.638/0.929, slightly better than predicted. The nine launch-bound workloads also improved (14.26-14.78us -> 12.91-13.88us, speedup 1.25-1.34x) because the tiny class stopped spreading 1024 elements over 8192 masked lanes and the 1M class moved to a larger tile. Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.8607 -> 1.1289 with all 36 workloads passing; the fp32 16M case at 0.93x while fp16/bf16 sit at 0.65x localizes the residual gap to the fp32 intermediate conversion, not to bandwidth.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Switch the low-precision elementwise math to the input dtype: the fp32 upcast/downcast makes the large fp16/bf16 workloads vector-op bound rather than bandwidth bound, which is why fp32 (no conversion) reaches 0.93x while fp16/bf16 reach only 0.65x. Triton's scalar rule already keeps `x * const` in the tensor's dtype, so removing the explicit fp32 round-trip should cut two of the four vector ops.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The harness measures per-iteration throughput with host and device overlapped: the large workloads now report ~28-31us, i.e. the device time alone, not device+host. Tile size is therefore the only lever for the large class and the launch path is the only lever for the rest.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 fixed the host path (0.861x, nine workloads above 1.2x). Round 3 fixed the tile for the device-bound class (1.129x). The remaining asymmetry is that fp32, which has no conversion, is already near reference bandwidth while fp16/bf16 are not.

plan.strategy: Evaluate the elementwise scaling in the input dtype instead of round-tripping fp16/bf16 through fp32
plan.code_changes: Both kernels changed from (x.to(tl.float32) * 57.29577951308232).to(x.dtype) to x * 57.29577951308232. Triton's scalar rule (scalar kind <= tensor kind does not participate in promotion) evaluates this in the input dtype, so fp16/bf16 avoid the fp32 round-trip while fp32 math is bit-identical to before. Launch path, tile ladder, cache keys and control flow unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three large fp32/bf16 cases are limited by the fp32 intermediate conversion rather than by memory traffic: fp32, which needs no conversion, already reaches 0.93x of the reference while otherwise identical fp16 and bf16 kernels reach only 0.650x and 0.638x

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the per-element vector work for the low-precision large tensors (remove upcast and downcast) should move the fp16/bf16 4096x4096 workloads from vector-op bound toward the 4.3TB/s bandwidth already reached by the conversion-free fp32 case

conclusion.root_cause: fp16 has native vector multiply on this backend, so removing the upcast/downcast cut two of four vector ops and raised throughput from 2.4TB/s to 3.2TB/s; bf16 multiply is evidently emulated through fp32 with truncation, so the same edit left its cost unchanged while degrading its accuracy.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: removing the fp32 round-trip moves the low-precision large workloads from vector-op bound toward reference bandwidth, lifting geo_mean. Observed per workload: the fp16 4096x4096 case went 27.85us -> 21.18us (speedup 0.650 -> 0.808) and its contract error became exactly 0, matching the prediction; the fp32 case was unchanged as expected (30.98us, 0.935); but the bf16 4096x4096 case did not move (29.91 -> 29.94us, 0.638) and its error grew from 0.0 to 0.0076 relative. Two of three groups behaved as predicted, so the aggregate only rose 1.1289 -> 1.1342, and the mechanism was only half confirmed.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Apply the input-dtype multiply only to fp16 and restore the fp32 round-trip for bf16 (and keep fp32 as is), selected by a compile-time dtype branch inside the kernel; this keeps the fp16 gain (21.18us, bit-exact) while returning bf16 to exact agreement at the same speed.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Dropping an explicit fp32 round-trip is only free where the backend has native low-precision vector ops: fp16 became bit-identical to the reference and 24% faster on the large case, while bf16 lost accuracy (max relative error 0.0079 in an independent probe, i.e. only 1.26x margin against the 1e-2 gate tolerance) without gaining any speed, which points to bf16 multiply being emulated through fp32 with truncation.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 fixed the launch path, round 3 fixed the tile, round 4 tried dtype-native arithmetic. The fp16 half of that idea is confirmed and should be kept; the bf16 half must be reverted because it trades accuracy for nothing.

series.title: 先优化随机数计算，再降低启动开销
series.note: 性能瓶颈随优化迁移：设备计算 → 宿主启动。

plan.strategy: Measure the unmodified seed (parent FlagGems uniform) to establish authoritative per-workload latency on this workspace.
plan.hypothesis: Baseline establishes the reference speedup for the 9 timing workloads; host RNG-state fetch and the Philox device path are the suspected dominant costs, to be separated by later rounds.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline measured: all 18 workloads pass, geo_mean 0.1520. Latency is flat ~0.350 ms for the three 1024-element cases (fp16/bf16/fp32) and ~0.345-0.351 ms for all three 65536-element cases, but 2.41-2.45 ms for the three 1048576-element cases. The flat 0.35 ms floor across element counts is host-side per-call cost (flag_gems philox_backend_seed_offset reads/writes generator state through device tensors), while the extra ~2.1 ms at 1M elements is the Philox/scale/store device kernel (same magnitude for fp16, bf16 and fp32, so the store conversion is not the driver).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline only, no prior measurement. Reference walltime is ~0.087-0.131 ms on every case, i.e. the reference call is launch-bound, so the whole gap is our own per-call cost: ~0.25 ms of avoidable host RNG-state work on the small cases and ~2.1 ms of device kernel time on the 1M cases (speedup 0.035-0.045 there).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Use a bounded debug job to read the installed flag_gems random_utils (philox_backend_seed_offset, uint_to_uniform_float) and the ascend _lean_seed_offset helper, time the host state-fetch path against initial_seed/get_offset/set_offset, and time kernel variants (tl.philox vs a manual uint32 Philox4x32-10) to locate the 2.1 ms/1M-element device cost before rewriting.

points.observation: 区分计算与状态读取成本

plan.strategy: Vectorize the Philox device path and remove launch-bound host overhead while repairing the two independent-gate semantic defects (dtype-exact lower clamp, contiguous output for strided input).
plan.code_changes: 1) Replaced tl.philox with a manual vectorized Philox4x32-10 in uint32 arithmetic (16-bit split multiply-high, masked low-word reconstruction) in the same counter/key layout as the seed. 2) Replaced the seed's in-kernel fp32 round-trip bound computation with host-computed, dtype-exact clamp bounds (smallest representable value >= from_, largest < to) passed as two float scalars, then clamped with min/max after the store conversion. 3) Output allocated contiguous via torch.empty(shape, dtype, device) so a strided self is handled. 4) Host RNG state via generator.initial_seed()/get_offset()/set_offset() advancing exactly grid*BLOCK counters, replacing philox_backend_seed_offset. 5) BLOCK = clamp(next_pow2(n/160), 64, 4096) with the heuristics decorator removed, so grid >= ~40 programs for large tensors.
plan.hypothesis: The seed device kernel is dominated by a scalarised tl.philox lowering (~350 us for one 1024-lane program, ~7x350 us for 1M elements) and the per-call host cost by the generator state ByteTensor round-trip; replacing both and fixing the two independent-gate semantic defects (missing nearest-dtype lower clamp, stride-unsafe output allocation) should cut small-case latency from ~0.35 ms toward ~0.13 ms and large-case latency from ~2.45 ms toward ~0.13 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: The seed spends ~0.25 us per lane inside a scalarised tl.philox (351 us for a single 1024-lane program) plus ~27 us of host RNG-state fetch and a stride-unsafe allocation; a vectorized Philox removes the device cost and the lean state API plus better-shaped blocks cut the launch-bound floor.

conclusion.root_cause: Two costs dominated the seed: (1) tl.philox is scalarised on this backend at ~0.25 us per lane (351 us for a single 1024-lane program; 1M elements = 7 waves x 350 us because only 40 vector cores process 256 programs), and (2) per-call host work, chiefly the generator state ByteTensor round-trip (27.1 us vs 0.90 us for initial_seed/get_offset/set_offset) plus a stride-unsafe empty_like. Replacing tl.philox with a vectorised manual Philox4x32-10 (identical to Random123's key schedule, 16-bit split multiply-high), taking the RNG offset through the lean API, allocating a contiguous output and choosing BLOCK so that ~40+ programs exist removed both, leaving only the ~70 us Triton launch overhead.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was a drop from ~0.35 ms to ~0.13 ms on the launch-bound cases and from ~2.45 ms to ~0.13 ms on the 1M cases; observed 0.111-0.116 ms and 0.116-0.120 ms, i.e. slightly better than predicted, and geo_mean rose 0.1520 -> 0.8924 (5.87x). Every case now sits 6-20 us above the reference call (0.093-0.115 ms), and latency is flat across 1024/65536/1048576 elements, so the remainder is per-call host work, dominated by the ~70 us Triton metacall. Round 1 measured that same launch floor at 58-64 us for a store-only kernel, which bounds the achievable gain from a naked launcher at roughly +50-60% on this metric.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the remaining ~70 us per-call Triton Python launch overhead: cache the CompiledKernel returned by the first launch and re-enter it through the backend launcher entry point (the probe reported it takes 18 arguments for this 8-argument kernel), keeping the plain kernel[grid](...) path as a fallback, so the launch-bound cases approach the reference's ~0.10 ms.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two independent-gate defects were invisible to the KG contract and had to be checked directly: (a) a float32 draw in [from, to) rounds below from in low precision, so the lower bound also needs a nearest-dtype clamp; (b) torch.empty_like on a strided self yields a non-contiguous buffer that a flat store pattern leaves partly uninitialised. Probe 4 also showed that an in-kernel comparison written as from_.to(DT).to(tl.float32) < from_ is folded to an identity, silently disabling the clamp; computing the bounds on the host removed that class of failure. The 16-bit multiply-high alternative was sound only after the CPU identity check exposed a wrong low-word reconstruction.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established a flat 0.35 ms floor across 1024/65536 elements with 2.41-2.45 ms at 1M, which excluded the store path and dtype conversion as causes. Bounded target probes then separated the device cost (scalarised tl.philox, 0.25 us/lane) from the host cost (state tensor round-trip) and from the Triton launch floor (~60 us for any kernel), so the rewrite targeted the RNG implementation and the wrapper rather than tiles or unroll factors.

plan.strategy: Replace the per-call Triton metacall with a cached direct launch of the compiled kernel.
plan.code_changes: Added a cached direct re-entry of the compiled kernel: the first call for a (dtype, numel, from_, to) shape still goes through kernel[grid](...) and captures the returned CompiledKernel; later calls invoke its backend entry with the same 9 leading arguments and the same 9 bound arguments that Triton's JITFunction.run builds (grid dims, current stream, entry point, packed metadata, launch-metadata/hook slots, then out, N, seed, offset, from_, span, lo, hi, BLOCK). The current stream is still read per call, no tensor or generator state is cached, and any exception falls back to the ordinary metacall. Kernel code and semantics are unchanged from round 2.
plan.hypothesis: All nine timing workloads are now launch-bound: the device work is a few microseconds and the flat ~0.115 ms per call is dominated by the ~62-71 us Triton metacall plus ~10-14 us of wrapper Python, so re-entering the already-compiled kernel with the argument vector Triton itself builds should remove most of that and bring every case at or below the reference's ~0.10 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: Round 2 latency is flat at 0.111-0.120 ms across 1024/65536/1048576 elements while the reference is 0.093-0.115 ms, so the residual gap is per-call host work; ~70 us of it is the metacall rebuild of bound arguments, specialisation and cache key, which a direct entry avoids.

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call latency was flat at 0.111-0.120 ms independent of element count because the Triton metacall rebuilds bound arguments, specialisation and the cache key on every launch (~62-71 us measured for this 8-argument kernel) on top of ~10-14 us of wrapper Python; the device work was only a few microseconds except at 1M elements.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was that launch-bound cases would fall at or below the reference's ~0.10 ms; observed 0.0678-0.0705 ms on the six small/medium cases and 0.0853-0.0880 ms on the three 1M cases, so geo_mean rose 0.8924 -> 1.4926 and every workload now beats the reference (min speedup 1.126). The gain is smaller than a naive subtraction of the whole ~70 us metacall, which is consistent with the wrapper's other host work (allocation, generator state, stream query) and with the 1M cases becoming limited by device execution (~85 us) once the host stopped gating them; the large-case speedups 1.13/1.13/1.28 are the new worst three and now reflect kernel time, not host time.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three 1048576-element cases are now device-bound at 0.085-0.088 ms (speedup 1.13-1.28) while the six smaller cases are 1.6-1.8, so the remaining headroom is in the kernel rather than the launch path: the Philox chain is ten serially dependent rounds per lane, so interleaving two independent counter chains per lane (eight outputs) with a correspondingly smaller BLOCK would expose instruction-level parallelism and could cut the large-case time, at the risk of unified-buffer pressure.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The decisive evidence was the shape of the latency curve, not any single measurement: a flat per-call cost across 1024/65536/1048576 with a ~0.25 us-per-lane spike only for the RNG path identified a scalarised builtin plus a metacall floor. Reading the installed JITFunction.run source gave the exact backend launcher argument layout (9 leading arguments plus all bound arguments including the constexpr), which was the only reliable way to re-enter the compiled kernel without guessing the private ABI.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 showed the cost is per-call, not per-element; probes then attributed it (scalarised tl.philox ~0.25 us/lane, state round-trip 27 us, metacall floor ~60 us). Round 2 removed the first two but left a flat ~0.115 ms, which this round's launch-path change removed; the residual split is now visible as 0.068 ms host-bound versus 0.085 ms device-bound at 1M, which redirects the next experiment from host dispatch to kernel ILP.

profile.summary: mixed: Six timing cases are host-bound: the 1024-element call costs 10.77 us of device time inside a 70.02 us eval call, and the device stream idles ~70 us between consecutive kernels, Three 1M-element cases are device-bound and vector-pipe bound: eval latency equals kernel duration, vector ratio 0.88-0.90 with MTE2 ~0 and MTE3 <=2.5%, The 1024-element case runs only 4 programs on a 20-core device, so per-program fixed cost dominates its 10.77 us device time

series.title: 分开解决小输入启动与大输入搬运
series.note: 两次修改针对不同尺寸区间；保留完整评测结果。

plan.strategy: Establish the authoritative baseline of the supplied seed implementation (contiguous 1-D negation kernel + collapsed-stride gather kernel) in this workspace
plan.code_changes: None: the seed file is evaluated unmodified
plan.hypothesis: The seed already passes all 30 workloads (a prior formal run of this exact file passed 30/30 with geo_mean 0.167); its cost is dominated by a ~55 us Triton launch path for small tensors and a 152 us BLOCK=4096 kernel for 4096x4096 tensors

expected_effect.mechanism: Records the starting point for later launch-overhead and tiling experiments

conclusion.root_cause: Seed cost structure established: 9 of 12 timing workloads are host-launch-bound (55-62 us measured against a 40-55 us Triton launch floor, with per-launch marginal cost measured at ~54 us) and 3 are device-bound (151.6 us for 4096x4096 with BLOCK=4096/grid=4096, i.e. ~0.9 TB/s effective on a 176 MB L2-resident working set where the aten reference reaches 23 us).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline geo_mean 0.1597, min_speedup 0.0830 (timing-3). All 30 workloads pass, confirming the earlier 27/30 flaggems baseline failure was not reproducible for this exact seed. Gap decomposition from paired target measurements: (a) launch path - an empty 1-tensor Triton launch costs 51.3 us while the same kernel through the compiled-kernel raw launcher costs 17.1 us and torch's in-place elementwise op costs 6-10 us, so ~35-45 us per call is pure Triton host overhead that dominates every small workload; (b) device tiling - the seed's BLOCK=4096 grid=4096 config measures 152 us on 4096x4096 fp32/fp16 whereas BLOCK=16384 grid=1024 measures 59.2/59.9 us (already at the then-host-bound floor), a 2.6x device-side gain.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Cut the per-call host cost by launching the precompiled Triton kernel directly (warmup once, then call the compiled runner with the tensor plus constexpr-specialized n), and retile large tensors to BLOCK=16384 so the device work drops under the new launch floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Bit-exact re-simulation of the frozen reference inputs showed the 3 reported non-finite mismatches do not reproduce; the only deviation was -0.0 vs +0.0 at index 0, which compare() accepts (|diff|=0 <= atol). A prior formal run of the identical file passed 30/30.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From prompt-only analysis (suspected strided-gather numerics bug) to paired target evidence: numerics are exact, the real cost is a ~55 us Triton host launch path plus an undersized device tile.

points.observation: 小输入约55 μs，大输入约152 μs
points.source_label_scope: Recorded information used or experimental background; independent causal contribution not quantified

plan.strategy: Remove Triton's per-call host launch overhead by launching the precompiled kernel through Triton's own compiled-kernel entry point, keeping identical device kernels and tiling
plan.code_changes: Split the seed kernel into _neg_exact (no mask) and _neg_tail (masked, other=0.0); keep a per-specialisation CompiledKernel handle (kernel.warmup) and launch it through the compiled-kernel entry point with (gridX,1,1, current stream, function, packed_metadata, t, constexprs), skipping the per-call JITFunction binding/cache lookup. Kernel bodies, tiling (BLOCK=4096 above 4096 elements, next_pow2 single tile below) and the strided gather kernel are unchanged, and the standard kernel[grid](...) call remains the fallback.
plan.hypothesis: If the ~55 us per-call cost of the 9 small workloads is Triton host-side launch overhead rather than device work, then launching the already compiled kernel directly (17.1 us measured for the same launch in probe2 vs 51.3 us through kernel[grid]) should cut those workloads to roughly 25-30 us and raise geo_mean from 0.16 to about 0.30, while the three 4096x4096 workloads stay device-bound at ~152 us because their tiling is unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes ~27 us of per-call Python argument binding/cache bookkeeping from the 9 host-bound workloads (n<=1048576), where device work is only a few microseconds

conclusion.root_cause: The 9 host-bound workloads were paying Triton's per-call Python launch overhead (measured 54.5 us marginal per empty launch, 51.3 us for a 1-tensor launch) on top of only a few microseconds of device work; replacing the JITFunction.run binding/cache path with the compiled-kernel entry point removed ~21-27 us per call.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted: 9 host-bound workloads fall from ~55-62 us to ~25-30 us (speedup ~0.30) and geo_mean ~0.30, with the three 4096x4096 workloads unchanged at ~152 us. Observed: geo_mean 0.2831 (+77% vs baseline 0.1597); the nine n<=1048576 workloads measured 31.1-34.5 us (speedup 0.336-0.448, previously 0.170-0.188) and the three 4096x4096 workloads stayed at 151.5/151.8/152.0 us (0.085/0.126/0.150), exactly as predicted. Residual gap versus the prediction: the isolated probe measured 27.4-28.9 us per call (best of 3 trials) whereas the harness records 31.1-34.5 us (median of 3 trials after a 25 ms warmup budget), i.e. ~4-6 us of additional per-call cost in the harness path, and the harness reference timings for the small workloads (11.0-12.9 us) are slower than my probe's (8.8-9.2 us), which raises the reference side and lowers speedup relative to my estimate. min_speedup is unchanged at 0.085 because timing-3 was deliberately left on the old tiling.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Retile the device kernel for large tensors: BLOCK=16384 (exact, mask-free) instead of BLOCK=4096/grid=4096, which probe2 measured at 59 us vs 152 us on 4096x4096, so the three still-device-bound workloads (currently 0.085/0.126/0.150 speedup) drop toward the new host floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-launch marginal cost measured 54.5 us for an empty Triton launch on this stack; the compiled-kernel entry point costs 17.1 us for the same launch, so on this operator the host path, not the elementwise math, is the primary optimization target for n<=1048576.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Layer 1 (host launch path) is now largely done; the remaining cost splits into ~31 us residual host path for small tensors and ~152 us device time for the three 4096x4096 tensors, which is where the worst speedup now lives.

plan.strategy: Retile the device kernel to one 64 KiB tile per program for large tensors, keeping the direct launch path
plan.code_changes: run() now picks block = 65536 // A.element_size() (16384 elements for fp32, 32768 for fp16/bf16 = one 64 KiB tile) when n > 4096, keeping next_pow2(n) single-tile for n <= 4096, with the same exact/masked kernel split and unchanged host launch path and strided kernel.
plan.hypothesis: If the 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound because a 16 KiB tile per program (BLOCK=4096, grid=4096) under-uses the vector core DMA, then a 64 KiB tile (BLOCK=16384 fp32 / 32768 fp16, grid=1024/512) should cut their latency from 152 us to roughly 34-42 us while the nine host-bound workloads stay at their current ~31-36 us, lifting geo_mean from 0.283 to about 0.42.

expected_effect.mechanism: Larger per-program DMA bursts and 4x fewer programs raise the device-side effective bandwidth of the 4096x4096 workloads from ~0.9 TB/s toward the aten reference's ~5 TB/s, dropping them from 152 us toward the ~33 us host floor

conclusion.root_cause: The 4096x4096 workloads were device-bound because a BLOCK=4096 tile moves only 16 KiB per program, so 4096 programs per kernel spend most of their time on per-program DMA setup rather than on payload; a 64 KiB tile (16384 fp32 / 32768 fp16 elements) reaches the DMA efficiency needed to fall back under the host launch floor.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted: 4096x4096 workloads drop from 152 us to roughly 34-42 us, the nine host-bound workloads keep ~31-36 us, geo_mean ~0.42. Observed: geo_mean 0.4129 (+46% vs 0.2831); the three 4096x4096 workloads fell from 151.5/151.8/152.0 us to 30.4/34.0/41.4 us (speedup 0.085/0.126/0.150 -> 0.412/0.563/0.548) and the nine others stayed at 29.8-31.5 us, matching the prediction within measurement noise. min_speedup improved from 0.084 to 0.366 and the worst workload is now a small host-bound one (timing-9) rather than a large device-bound one, i.e. the device-tiling bottleneck is gone and the residual gap is the host launch floor plus fp32 4096x4096 device time (41.4 us vs the 30 us floor).
conclusion.next_suggestion: With 11 of 12 workloads now inside a few microseconds of the ~30 us host launch floor, attack the remaining host cost: probe6 showed the same launch costs 12.3 us when the pointer is passed as an integer address and the stream handle is resolved through a pre-resolved torch_npu._C entry point, versus 22.8 us with a tensor argument and the driver registry lookup per call.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this stack a 64 KiB tile per program is the largest element-wise tile that stays inside the vector core UB: fp32 tiles of 32768 elements and static_range loops of 4-8 tiles did not merely fail to compile, they poisoned the device (vector core exception) while still returning plausible timings, so UB sizing must be validated explicitly rather than inferred from a fast measurement.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Device tiling is now resolved (64 KiB tiles); the binding constraint has moved back to the per-call host cost, which now sets the latency of 11 of 12 workloads, with fp32 4096x4096 still ~10 us above that floor.

profile.summary: mixed: Nine of twelve timed workloads are dispatch-bound: device task time is 1.5-5.2 us while eval latency is 30.3-31.5 us, 4096x4096 fp32 is device-bound with fully serialized AIV pipes (MTE2+MTE3+VEC+scalar sum equals aiv_time), 64 KiB tiles already sustain ~5.9 TB/s aggregate MTE2 read rate (L2-resident); per-program DMA width is not the residual limit

plan.strategy: Measure the provided best-so-far selu_ candidate unchanged to establish the authoritative baseline
plan.code_changes: None; seed written verbatim (buffered Triton elementwise kernels + cached raw Ascend launcher path + constexpr-stride generic kernel for non-contiguous inputs)
plan.hypothesis: The seed's cached raw launcher minimizes host overhead; its 8192-element tile caps vector-core occupancy, so large shapes leave bandwidth and small shapes leave launch latency on the table

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; records reference candidate latency for all 12 timing workloads

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline recorded. Two independent cost centers, both measured: (1) 9 of 12 timing workloads are host-launch bound and flat at ~16.1-17.5us regardless of numel (fp32: 16.110us at numel=1024 vs 16.112us at numel=1048576). Debug measurement on the target splits this into a 12.25us raw Ascend launcher call plus ~2.1us of avoidable Python dispatch in run() (numel/is_contiguous/data_ptr/tuple/dict), on top of which the harness adds ~1.4us; the framework reference launches in 8.65us. (2) The 3 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound at ~82-83us and the device cost is a fixed ~1.5us per TILE, not a bandwidth or vector-throughput limit: fp16 (67MB) and fp32 (134MB) take the same 82-83us, a pure copy kernel costs the same as the SELU kernel at the same tile size, and cost scales with tile COUNT (selu fp16 at BLOCK 1024/2048/4096/8192 = 607/300/160/82us). A 16384 tile halves the tile count and halves device time (pure copy 78us -> 40us), but the 192KB UB budget with auto multi-buffering blocks a 16384 tile for fp32 and bf16.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Two evidence-backed levers, in expected-value order. First the host path, which governs 9 of 12 workloads: replace the per-call Python dispatch with an object-identity fast path so a repeated tensor skips numel/is_contiguous/data_ptr/tuple/dict (~2.1us measured), and keep the raw launcher (graph replay was measured slower at 46us and numerically incorrect, so it is discarded). Second the device path: give fp16 a 16384-element tile with native-precision math (verified max_abs 0.0039 vs the 0.015 atol), which measured 46.5us vs 82us for the 4096x4096 case; bf16 and fp32 must stay at 8192 because every 16384 formulation and every num_stages=2 pipelined loop overflows UB, and num_stages>2 is rejected by the compiler.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Pipelined-loop timing at 40+ iterations cannot resolve device cost; measuring through the cheap raw launcher with a known host floor, plus dtype and tile-size sweeps, isolated a per-TILE latency model (~1.5us/tile/40 vector cores) that predicted the pure-copy result exactly. Per-call torch.npu.synchronize() adds a ~50us constant and must not be used for absolute latency.

plan.strategy: Collapse the per-call host dispatch to a single object-identity test plus a fully pre-bound raw launch
plan.code_changes: run() now keeps a (tensor-object, zero-argument launch) pair: when the same tensor object is passed again it dispatches straight through the pre-bound launch behind one identity test. The per-specialization launch also bakes the integer data pointer (the raw launcher accepts an int for a tensor parameter), so the cache key becomes (dtype, numel, aligned, ptr) and no per-call argument is rebuilt. Kernels, tiles and math are byte-identical to round 1, and non-contiguous/misaligned calls keep ordinary Triton launches.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of twelve timing workloads are purely host-launch bound and flat in numel, so cutting the ~2.1us of measured Python dispatch per call raises only those nine and leaves the three 4096x4096 device-bound workloads unchanged

expected_effect.mechanism: Target debug timing showed run()'s per-call Python dispatch (dtype/numel/data_ptr tuple, dict lookup, closure arguments) cost ~2.1us on top of the 12.25us raw launcher, so removing it should drop the nine launch-bound workloads from ~16.1us toward ~13-14us

conclusion.root_cause: The nine launch-bound workloads were paying per-call Python dispatch (dtype/numel/data_ptr tuple construction, dict lookup, and argument marshalling into the launcher) on top of the raw launch. Binding the data pointer into the specialization and short-circuiting a repeated tensor behind one identity test removed it. The three 4096x4096 workloads are untouched because they are device-bound by per-TILE latency, not host-bound: 2048 tiles of 8192 elements at ~1.5us each over 40 vector cores.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted the nine launch-bound workloads would fall from ~16.1-17.5us toward ~13-14us; they fell further, to 9.0-10.4us, so the gap vs prediction is favourable (about 4us better than forecast) and every one of the nine now exceeds the reference (speedups 1.03-1.23 vs 0.72-0.84). The per-call Python dispatch removed was larger in the real harness than the 2.1us measured in isolation, which is consistent with the harness's own per-call wrapper being charged once per iteration rather than once per debug loop. The three 4096x4096 workloads are unchanged within noise (81.6/83.2/82.7us vs 81.9/83.2/82.7us baseline, speedups 0.696/0.710/0.597 vs 0.694/0.710/0.598), exactly as predicted for a purely host-side change, and they are now the whole remaining deficit: 2.4us of it is the host launch floor and ~77us is the device term of 2048 tiles x ~1.5us / 40 vector cores.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Take the device side next, which is now the only remaining gap (timing-3/7/11 at 0.696/0.710/0.597 while all nine host-bound workloads already exceed parity). Give fp16 a 16384-element tile with native-precision math: it halves the tile count, measured 46.5us vs 82us pre-regression on the same shape, and its accuracy was verified at max_abs 0.0039 against a 0.015 atol. In the same probe series, test whether passing the destination as a second pointer parameter removes a conservative aliasing serialization that could be the source of the ~1.5us per-tile latency, which is the only route left to help bf16 and fp32 at their UB-capped 8192 tile.

plan.strategy: Collapse the per-call host path to one dict lookup, two new_empty allocations, one unbind split and one pre-bound raw compiled-kernel launch.
plan.code_changes: Wrapper only: single dict lookup keyed on (dtype, shape, stride, N, C, group, eps, weight.dtype, bias.dtype); both outputs allocated with x.new_empty (no dtype/device kwarg parsing); mean/rstd from one buf.unbind(0) instead of two selects; launch goes through the captured ck.run.launch with all 10 shape/stride constexprs and eps pre-bound, passing tensor args so no Python data_ptr extraction; stream getter resolved once.
plan.hypothesis: Per-call host cost dominates (device kernel is ~6.5us and the score is flat across a 16x data-size range), so cutting Python glue, view dispatches and allocation-kwarg parsing lowers every workload's walltime by roughly the same constant and raises geo_mean toward ~0.8.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes ~11us of per-call wrapper glue, ~2.5us of a second select dispatch, and any dtype/device kwarg parsing from the 2 allocations, leaving only the ~23.3us raw launch plus 2 allocs.

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call walltime is dominated by this runtime's compiled-kernel launch path (~39us even for a no-op kernel, ~+1.1us per launch argument), not by wrapper glue or allocation dispatches; the 26-slot launch of the 17-argument signature measured 48.0us against a 35.2us torch reference in the same process.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was ~12us of host savings per call from trimming wrapper glue, a second select dispatch and allocation kwarg parsing, i.e. geo_mean toward ~0.8. Observed geo_mean 0.582 vs 0.592 baseline, with per-workload candidate/reference ratios flat (mean 1.71 vs 1.70) even though both sides were ~28% slower in absolute terms than round 1 (reference 41.4-50.0us vs 32.6-36.8us), so the round is ratio-comparable and the savings did not materialize. A follow-up min-of-reps A/B in one process showed why: the compiled launch entry alone costs ~48us for the 17-argument signature and a no-op 1-argument Triton launch still costs ~38.7us, while an extra launch argument costs ~1.1us (no-op with 19 total args: 49.0us). The wrapper work I removed was largely absorbed under that blocking launch cost (allocations interleaved with a launch cost only ~6.7us of the ~18us they cost standalone).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Cut the launch argument count itself: generate, once per specialization, a kernel whose geometry/strides/BLOCK/COUNT/eps are literals so the signature is 5 tensor args (14 launch slots) instead of 17 (26 slots), merge mean/rstd into one packed buffer pointer, and pick the cheapest compiled launch entry at build time.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Measurement moved from a single-shot probe to a load-robust min-of-reps A/B in one process, which separated the irreducible launch floor from removable argument/allocation cost and redirected the next change from wrapper glue to the kernel signature itself.

plan.strategy: Shrink the launch signature itself by inlining all geometry into a generated kernel and tune the launch entry, instead of trimming wrapper glue.
plan.code_changes: New wrapper path: per-specialization generated Triton kernel whose HW/CG/NS/CS/SS/BLOCK/COUNT/eps/NG are literals, so the kernel signature is (X, OUT, BUF, W, B) = 5 tensor args (14 launch slots) instead of 17 args (26 slots); mean and rstd share one packed (2,N,group) buffer pointer; the compiled entry (ck.run vs ck.run.launch) is chosen once at build time by timing 16 real launches; fast path is one dict lookup + two new_empty + one unbind + one pre-bound launch. The general _gn_kernel is retained with a raw-launch and a plain-JIT fallback if generation fails.
plan.hypothesis: Measured launch-argument cost (~1.1us per slot from 10 vs 19 total slots on no-op kernels) means collapsing 26 launch slots to 14 should cut ~10us of per-call host time, moving candidate latency from ~58us toward ~48us and geo_mean from 0.59 to ~0.7.

expected_effect.mechanism: 12 fewer launch slots at ~1.1us each plus removal of per-call stream/entry overhead lowers the launch component from ~48us toward the ~39us no-op floor, which is a constant saving on every workload.

conclusion.root_cause: Two host-side costs swamped the argument-count saving: the noisy 16-iteration entry tuner usually picked the slower NPULauncher call entry (+3.8us), and calling the raw stream getter on every launch is serialized against the runtime's launch path (+9.8us). The remaining wrapper cost is allocation and view dispatch, not the launch.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: 12 fewer launch slots at ~1.1us each plus a tuned entry would take candidate latency from ~58us toward ~48us (geo_mean ~0.7). Observed geo_mean 0.547 with candidate mean 61.5us versus round 1's 56.9us at an identical reference load (reference mean 33.62us in both rounds), i.e. the change made the candidate 4.6us worse instead of 10us better, although all 27 workloads including the generated kernels' numerics passed. A same-process diagnostic on the built candidate explained the gap: the build-time tuner selected ck.run (NPULauncher __call__) at 30.78us instead of ck.run.launch at 26.99us, and the per-call stream getter cost far more inside the launch loop than standalone (0.83us standalone) - the same 5-argument launch with a captured stream int measured 17.24us. The wrapper itself still adds 27.9us over the bare launch (wrapper_batch 54.9us vs entry_launch_batch 27.0us vs ref_batch 27.0us).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Pin ck.run.launch and cache the stream handle per specialization, which the diagnostic measured as 3.8us plus 9.8us per call, then attack the remaining wrapper overhead (two new_empty allocations plus one unbind, which accounted for the 27.9us gap between the bare launch and the full wrapper).
conclusion.debug_lesson: The per-specialization tuner was harmful because 16-iteration min comparisons cannot separate entries that differ by ~15%, and a runtime query that looks negligible standalone can be serialized against the launch queue; both must be measured inside the real per-call path.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Launch-entry selection must be deterministic rather than timing-selected, and the stream handle must be captured once per specialization; allocation/view dispatch is now the largest removable wrapper term.
